Facebook X Whatsapp E-mail Linkedin Researchers say bacteria-carrying mosquitoes could strengthen existing disease-control efforts. AP Washington: Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday. The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here. In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team. The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. “This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Are you a mosquito magnet? Scientists reveal why you get bitten more Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. How special mosquitoes help fight dengue How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus. The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease. linked to 69% drop in dengue, chikungunya infections Study of 5,700 children offers fresh hope in the fight against mosquito-borne viruses Last updated: November 21, 2026 | 19:02 AP 2 MIN READ Follow on Whatsapp Follow on Google Follow on Telegram https://gulfnews.com/lifestyle/health-fitness/special-mosquitoes-linked-to-69-drop-in-dengue-chikungunya-infections-1.500756332 Link Copied!! Facebook X Whatsapp E-mail Linkedin Researchers say bacteria-carrying mosquitoes could strengthen existing disease-control efforts. AP Washington: Children who lived in Brazilian neighborhoods buzzing with a special kind of mosquito were far less likely to catch dengue or another worrisome virus, chikungunya, researchers reported Saturday. The major study of more than 5,700 children in one of the world’s dengue hot spots offers new evidence that breeding mosquitoes unable to transmit these viruses can be a viable strategy rather than solely relying on pesticides and trying to avoid getting bitten. Get updated faster and for FREE: Download the Gulf News app now - simply click here. In neighborhoods populated by these so-called Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes, researchers found about a 69% reduction in dengue and chikungunya infections in schoolchildren compared to similar neighborhoods — an effect sustained even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak, said Dr. Sri Edupuganti of Emory University, part of the international research team. The researchers reported the findings at a meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene. “This is really exciting,” said Dr. David Hamer, a global health expert at Boston University who wasn’t involved with the Brazilian study. He predicts that pairing more use of these Wolbachia mosquitoes with existing steps to fight mosquito-borne disease could “knock dengue down to much lower levels” in many places. The latest research comes as Florida grapples with an unusually large outbreak of the virus, what appears to be the biggest in any U.S. state since at least the 1940s. Usually in the continental U.S., dengue is found mostly in people who traveled internationally. But as of Friday, Florida health officials had tallied more than 650 locally acquired cases, about three-quarters of them in Hillsborough County, home to Tampa. Are you a mosquito magnet? Scientists reveal why you get bitten more Outside the U.S., the nonprofit World Mosquito Program has pioneered the Wolbachia strategy. How special mosquitoes help fight dengue How it works: Scientists breed mosquitoes to carry a kind of bacteria called Wolbachia. It is harmless to people and common in many insects, although not dengue-carrying Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. The bacteria dramatically reduce the mosquitoes’ ability to transmit certain viruses. Female mosquitoes spread the bacteria to their offspring, so releasing enough of the specially bred insects — males and females — into an area allows Wolbachia to gradually become established in the local mosquito population. Field trials and other studies in Indonesia and elsewhere have shown the strategy can significantly lower dengue diagnoses. But because people with mild symptoms may not be diagnosed, the new study in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, went further. Researchers tested blood for signs of dengue, chikungunya or the Zika virus. The four-year study compared children living in neighborhoods that all got the same pesticide and other mosquito-control interventions, but half were randomly assigned to have Wolbachia mosquitoes released into the area. There were too few cases of Zika to calculate if the special mosquitoes had any effect on that disease. news.title_zh: 与登革热、基孔肯雅热感染下降69%相关的特殊蚊子 - 《海湾新闻》
news.source_body_en: A study published in Gulf News on November 21, 2026, highlights a 69% drop in dengue and chikungunya infections among over 5,700 children in Belo Horizonte, Brazil, where Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes were released. The research, presented at the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene meeting, suggests that these special mosquitoes could be a viable strategy to combat mosquito-borne viruses, reducing the need for reliance on pesticides. The study found that neighborhoods with Wolbachia mosquitoes had significantly fewer infections compared to similar areas without them, even during Brazil’s severe 2024 dengue outbreak. However, the impact on Zika virus cases could not be determined due to insufficient data. The World Mosquito Program has been working on this strategy globally, with field trials in Indonesia showing promising results. This development offers new hope for disease control efforts, particularly in regions heavily affected by dengue and chikungunya.
news.content_zh: 一项于2026年11月21日发表在《海湾新闻》上的研究指出,在巴西伯利奥尼市(Belo Horizonte)超过5700名儿童所在的地区,释放携带沃尔巴克氏体(Wolbachia)的蚊子后,登革热和基孔肯雅热感染率下降了69%。这项研究在美洲热带医学与卫生学会(American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene)会议上展示,表明这些特殊蚊子可能成为对抗蚊媒病毒的有效策略,减少对农药的依赖。研究发现,释放携带沃尔巴克氏体蚊子的社区与未释放的类似社区相比,感染病例显著减少,即使在巴西2024年严重的登革热暴发期间也是如此。然而,由于数据不足,无法确定该策略对寨卡病毒病例的影响。世界蚊子计划(World Mosquito Program)正在全球范围内推进这一策略,印尼的实地试验显示了积极的结果。这一进展为疾病控制工作带来了新的希望,特别是在登革热和基孔肯雅热高发地区。

news.excerpt: 2025年,中国广东省等地暴发了前所未有的大规模基孔肯雅热疫情,造成超过2.5万人感染。面对这一突发的公共卫生危机,研究团队希望能迅速查明此次疫情肆虐背后的病毒学与免疫学驱动因素,特别是探明病毒是否通过基因突变逃避了人体抗体识别,以及宿主群体中是否存在特定的遗传易感性。从而为制定精准的防疫政策、更新诊断试剂,以及针对特定人群“免疫缺口”设计下一代高效疫苗提供坚实的科学依据。 导 读 2025 ...

analysis.location_and_population: China, with a focus on the Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) outbreak and its antigenic and genetic analysis.
analysis.event: An antigenic and genetic analysis of the 2025 Chikungunya virus outbreak in China was conducted and published in The Innovation Life, with findings related to the East/Central/South African lineage (ECSA) of CHIKV.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The study reported over 3,000 cases of CHIKV infection in China during 2025, with a focus on the ECSA lineage. The analysis highlighted the potential for immune evasion and the role of specific HLA alleles in disease progression, but no explicit risk level was stated in the evidence.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The study was published in The Innovation Life and included detailed analysis of the outbreak. It referenced data from multiple sources, including GISAID, and discussed the implications of the genetic and antigenic characteristics of the virus. No unresolved information was reported in the evidence.

analysis.brief_en: The article reports on an antigenic and genetic analysis of the 2025 Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) outbreak in China, published in The Innovation Life. The study focused on the East/Central/South African lineage (ECSA) of CHIKV, which was identified as the dominant strain during the outbreak. It noted that over 3,000 cases were reported in China, with the virus showing potential for immune evasion. The research also examined the role of specific HLA alleles, such as HLA-C*07:02 and HLA-C*01:02, in disease progression. The findings were based on data from GISAID and other sources, and the study was conducted between 2025-01-18 and 2026-09-08. No explicit risk level was stated, but the analysis provided insights into the virus's behavior and its implications for public health responses.

news.content_zh: 文章报道了《The Innovation Life》上发表的一项关于2025 基孔肯雅病毒(CHIKV) 暴发在中国的抗原和基因组分析研究。该研究聚焦于CHIKV的东/中/南非系(ECSA),该病毒株在暴发期间被确认为主要流行株。文章指出,中国报告了超过3,000例病例,病毒显示出潜在的免疫逃逸能力。研究还探讨了特定HLA等位基因,如HLA-C*07:02和HLA-C*01:02,在疾病进展中的作用。研究结果基于GISAID和其他来源的数据,研究时间跨度为2025-01-18至2026-09-08。文章未明确提及风险等级,但分析提供了病毒行为及其对公共卫生应对措施的潜在影响的见解。

supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, November 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Pediatric Chikungunya Encephalitis Cases Documented in Northern Thailand With Complete Recoveries by November 23, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Pediatric Chikungunya Encephalitis Cases Documented in Northern Thailand With Complete Recoveries Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Medical researchers in northern Thailand have documented two distinct presentations of chikungunya-associated encephalitis in pediatric patients, demonstrating that acute central nervous system invasion by the mosquito-borne pathogen can occur across divergent stages of childhood development. The clinical report details the courses of a term neonate who acquired the virus through vertical maternal-fetal transmission and an eleven-year-old child who contracted the infection via a community-acquired mosquito bite in Hang Dong District, Chiang Mai Province. Despite presenting at opposing ends of the pediatric age spectrum with marked differences in clinical manifestations and laboratory indices, both patients achieved complete neurological recovery without long-term deficits following targeted supportive care. While the viral infection is historically considered self-limiting in healthy adults, severe and potentially life-threatening complications are increasingly documented in vulnerable populations, particularly neonates, young infants, and individuals with chronic medical comorbidities. Neurological involvement represents one of the most serious spectrums of clinical complications, encompassing encephalopathy, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, myelitis, and encephalitis. Encephalitis and encephalopathy carry substantial risks of severe morbidity and mortality, disproportionately burdening pediatric cohorts, especially newborns exposed peripartum. The setting of the documented cases underscores regional arboviral dynamics within Thailand, where chikungunya transmission remains endemic and surges during the seasonal monsoon rains spanning June through September. In 2025, Chiang Mai Province reported 484 diagnosed cases of chikungunya, representing an incidence rate of 30 infections per 100,000 population and placing the province third nationally in overall disease burden. Within this regional epidemiological landscape, Hang Dong District emerged as an intense focal point of transmission, recording 319 cases across two documented outbreaks and establishing the province’s highest localized incidence at 346 cases per 100,000 population. The two documented pediatric cases arose directly from this concentrated community outbreak setting. The first clinical case involved a male neonate delivered at term through an uncomplicated vaginal delivery to a mother who developed high-grade fever, rash, and severe joint pain two days prior to childbirth. The mother resided in an active outbreak zone where multiple household members experienced matching symptoms, leading to a maternal clinical diagnosis of chikungunya. Although born without apparent neurological abnormalities, the infant remained hospitalized for neonatal jaundice related to suboptimal feeding and required phototherapy. On day five of life, the neonate developed a high-grade fever of 38.9 degrees Celsius along with diffuse edema across all extremities. Recognizing the acute maternal history, clinicians suspected vertically acquired chikungunya virus infection, initiated supportive interventions, and collected serum for diagnostic evaluation. By day eight of life, the infant’s condition deteriorated as he exhibited marked lethargy, poor feeding, severe irritability, and decreased spontaneous motor movement across all four extremities, prompting urgent investigation for chikungunya-associated encephalitis. A lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis with 44 white blood cells per cubic millimeter consisting of 39 percent neutrophils and 61 percent lymphocytes, accompanied by a mildly elevated protein level of 147 milligrams per deciliter, normal glucose of 57 milligrams per deciliter, and 2,000 red blood cells per cubic millimeter from a traumatic tap. Molecular testing of both serum and cerebrospinal fluid confirmed the presence of chikungunya viral RNA using real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction, while assays for dengue virus, Zika virus, and bacterial cultures returned negative. During supportive inpatient therapy, the neonate developed prominent facial and perioral hyperpigmentation, a characteristic cutaneous manifestation recognized as the Chik sign, which progressively expanded to encompass the extremities before undergoing superficial desquamation. His hospitalization extended to 28 days due to an intercurrent episode of hospital-acquired pneumonia, which resolved with medical management. Longitudinal clinical evaluations conducted at six and twelve months of follow-up demonstrated age-appropriate neurological development and normal clinical examinations, verifying complete recovery without residual sequelae. The second case documented a community-acquired mosquito-borne infection in a previously healthy eleven-year-old boy who presented after a single day of acute high-grade fever reaching 38.6 degrees Celsius, lower-extremity myalgia, and rapidly progressive encephalopathy. His family resided in the same outbreak district, and his mother had recently recovered from a clinically diagnosed chikungunya episode. Physical evaluation revealed bilateral non-purulent conjunctival injection and an extensive erythematous morbilliform rash spanning his face, trunk, and extremities without concomitant arthritis or organomegaly. Diagnostic laboratory tests demonstrated marked systemic inflammation with leukocytosis totaling 13,100 white blood cells per cubic millimeter with 83 percent neutrophils, elevated aspartate aminotransferase of 94 units per liter, alanine aminotransferase of 62 units per liter, and serum creatine kinase elevated to 508 units per liter. In contrast to the neonatal presentation, lumbar puncture in the older child revealed clear cerebrospinal fluid devoid of pleocytosis, showing only 4 white blood cells per cubic millimeter, normal protein of 21 milligrams per deciliter, and normal glucose of 71 milligrams per deciliter. Brain magnetic resonance imaging performed on the seventh day of illness was unremarkable, yet real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction detected chikungunya viral RNA within both serum and cerebrospinal fluid, confirming direct viral neuroinvasion. Molecular confirmation across both patients relied on a commercial multiplex real-time reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction assay targeting the non-structural protein 1 gene of chikungunya virus, alongside control screening channels for the envelope gene of Zika virus and the three-prime non-coding region of dengue virus. The protocol utilized an analytical detection threshold of at least ten viral RNA copies per reaction, performing reverse transcription at 45 degrees Celsius followed by 45 thermal cycles of denaturation and annealing. In both instances, negative assays for co-circulating arboviruses and negative blood and cerebrospinal fluid bacterial cultures ruled out common secondary infectious etiologies, establishing chikungunya as the primary causative agent driving central nervous system inflammation. Lacking approved pathogen-specific antiviral therapies, patient care centered entirely on timely supportive interventions, hemodynamic stabilization, neurological surveillance, and empirical antimicrobial coverage that was discontinued upon negative microbial cultures. Within 24 hours of admission, the eleven-year-old patient regained full consciousness, and his elevated muscle enzymes normalized before discharge on hospital day seven. Together, these pediatric cases emphasize the critical necessity for pediatricians and public health clinicians to maintain a heightened diagnostic index of suspicion for chikungunya neuroinvasion during outbreak seasons, especially among neonates born to febrile mothers and children with abrupt neurological decompensation. The biological mechanisms driving chikungunya-associated neurological injury remain incompletely understood, but clinical evidence suggests a multifactorial pathway combining direct viral neuroinvasion with immune-mediated tissue damage. Detection of viral genetic material within cerebrospinal fluid and neural tissue demonstrates that chikungunya virus can directly breach the central nervous system. In tandem with direct viral replication, an exaggerated release of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines is thought to disrupt blood-brain barrier integrity, intensifying neuroinflammation and accelerating clinical encephalopathy. Mother-to-child transmission was first identified as a major source of severe neonatal infection during the 2005 to 2006 outbreak on Réunion Island, where maternal viremia around the time of delivery resulted in vertical transmission in approximately 50 percent of exposed newborns. While infants typically appear healthy at birth, clinical illness consistently surfaces between days three and seven of life. A meta-analysis established that nearly half of vertically infected neonates suffer neurological complications, conferring a 1.9-fold higher risk of adverse long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes compared with unexposed infants. Brain imaging in severe neonatal infections frequently identifies diffuse white-matter damage with splenial diffusion restriction, which may ultimately progress to cavitary lesions or cerebral atrophy. By comparison, community-acquired mosquito-borne encephalitis in older children remains less thoroughly characterized, though historical outbreak records highlight notable clinical vulnerability. During the Réunion Island epidemic, acute encephalitis occurred in 40 percent of hospitalized pediatric patients, while encephalopathy was documented in 13 percent, typically emerging within 24 hours of fever onset. Neuroimaging remains unremarkable in many pediatric presentations, though severe cases can manifest abnormalities in limbic structures or white matter, and between 10 and 20 percent of affected children suffer mortality or enduring neurological sequelae. Diagnostic evaluation requires a high index of suspicion and careful timing, as reverse-transcription polymerase chain reaction detects acute viremia, whereas virus-specific immunoglobulin M and G antibodies become clinically useful later in the disease course. Clinicians emphasize that while viral detection in cerebrospinal fluid establishes neuroinvasion, a negative fluid assay does not exclude central nervous system infection. In the absence of targeted antiviral therapies, patient management centers on neurological monitoring, seizure control, fluid and electrolyte stabilization, and intensive supportive care. At the population level, public health authorities in Thailand reinforce seasonal prevention during the monsoon rains through personal protective barriers, bed nets, insect repellents, and the systematic elimination of localized mosquito breeding habitats. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Tuesday, November 24, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Global Scoping Review Reveals Climate Warming Accelerates Chikungunya Transmission and Geographic Expansion by November 20, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Global Scoping Review Reveals Climate Warming Accelerates Chikungunya Transmission and Geographic Expansion Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A comprehensive scoping review evaluating a quarter-century of international research indicates that global climate change is actively altering the transmission intensity and geographical boundaries of the chikungunya virus. Led by Chao Wang, Xinyao Li, and colleagues, the systematic evaluation synthesized empirical climatic drivers, predictive ecological niche models, and public health adaptation strategies from 104 eligible studies published between January 1, 2000, and November 1, 2025. The investigators determined that while temperature and rainfall heavily modulate the biological kinetics of vector mosquitoes and viral replication, international research and preventive preparedness remain structurally imbalanced, leaving low-income and historically endemic regions vulnerable to escalating disease risks. Historically confined to localized tropical reservoirs following its initial identification in Tanzania during the 1950s, chikungunya virus—an arbovirus of the genus Alphavirus primarily transmitted by Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes—has rapidly expanded across the globe. Driven by climatic variability and heightened human mobility, autochthonous transmission has now been confirmed in more than 100 countries and territories. The pathogen has demonstrated substantial geographic momentum, initiating major epidemics across Southeast Asia, South Asia, Indian Ocean islands, and the Americas, where a continuous wave of infection took hold after late 2013. A significant surge documented in July 2025 led to more than 10,000 confirmed cases in Foshan, Guangdong, China, by the end of August, marking the country’s largest outbreak on record and underscoring how changing weather parameters amplify transmission in subtropical areas. The methodological framework of the review adhered strictly to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines, following an a priori protocol registered on the Open Science Framework. The researchers performed multi-database searches across PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and EBSCOhost, screening 2,336 initial records down to 104 qualifying English-language studies based on the Population, Concept, and Context framework. Methodological quality was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute Critical Appraisal Checklist, and the identified literature was categorized into empirical observations quantifying direct climatic impacts, future mathematical projections, and adaptation measures organized in alignment with the World Health Organization Global Arbovirus Initiative framework. A critical temporal analysis of the literature demonstrated an abrupt surge in research output over the last decade. Between 2000 and 2014, global scientific databases cataloged a mere seven qualifying studies examining climate-related chikungunya dynamics. From 2015 onward, publication numbers expanded dramatically to 97 articles, spurred in substantial part by the release of milestone assessments including the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change Fifth Assessment Report in 2014 and the Lancet Commission on Health and Climate Change in 2015. These international scientific syntheses catalyzed widespread efforts to measure the explicit epidemiological outcomes of atmospheric warming on arboviral spread, while shifting outbreak clusters in temperate Asian regions during 2025 subsequently spurred local empirical research interest. Synthesizing the empirical evidence across 48 climate-association studies, the researchers identified ambient temperature as the fundamental environmental driver of viral dissemination. Among 38 studies analyzing ambient thermal parameters, 36 reported a positive correlation with transmission metrics, while two documented suppressive effects under extreme conditions. Through a narrative synthesis of these investigations, the authors established a consolidated optimal transmission window between 23 degrees Celsius and 30 degrees Celsius. Within this specific thermal band, elevated temperatures accelerate viral replication, significantly shorten the extrinsic incubation period of the virus within mosquito hosts, enhance vector population growth, and increase adult survival rates. Conversely, temperatures falling below 17 degrees Celsius markedly reduce vector competence, whereas extreme heat exceeding 35 degrees Celsius diminishes mosquito survival and impairs the catalytic activity of viral ribonucleic acid polymerase. Rainfall and hydrological variations demonstrated a complex, dual effect across 32 analyzed studies, with 15 reporting positive correlations, 15 documenting negative associations, and two identifying geographically divergent outcomes. Moderate precipitation establishes standing water reserves essential for mosquito reproduction and larval development, with soil moisture anomalies directly enhancing transmission potential in tropical semi-arid zones. However, excessive precipitation and heavy storms produce a flushing effect that mechanically washes out established aquatic habitats, an inhibitory phenomenon particularly pronounced in high-altitude montane environments. Similarly, severe moisture deficits suppress dissemination by desiccating oviposition sites. Despite these opposing local mechanisms, the synthesis revealed a consistent biological time lag of one to four weeks between major precipitation events and corresponding spikes in clinical human cases. Atmospheric humidity was investigated in 11 studies, where moderate to elevated relative humidity was largely shown to extend larval survival, prolong breeding site stability, and increase egg production, as observed in field investigations across Iran and Spain. Conversely, persistently high relative humidity exceeding 70 percent demonstrated negative correlations with vector propagation in certain mid-to-high latitude settings, such as southern Brazil, illustrating that environmental suppression occurs when moisture conditions exceed the physiological adaptation range of local mosquito species. However, the review noted that empirical evaluations of non-thermal variables remain scarce, with factors like wind direction, wind speed, and microclimatic ground moisture largely neglected in published literature despite their clear influence on passive vector dispersal and larval habitat persistence. Beyond historical associations, six empirical investigations provided documented evidence that ongoing climate change has already altered local disease ecology. Longitudinal field data from Ecuador spanning 1988 to 2024 revealed that mosquito habitats advanced northward by 45 kilometers per decade, as warmer winters lowered egg mortality and yielded a 2.5-fold increase in locally acquired cases in temperate highland areas. In Brazil’s tropical savanna, concurrent heatwaves and altered rainfall regimes boosted transmission intensity by 30 percent compared to stable baseline periods. Similarly, prior to the large 2025 outbreak in Foshan, China, the region experienced 38 cumulative days of suitable mosquito propagation conditions, including an unbroken 23-day peak window that directly facilitated widespread community transmission. Evaluating 50 forward-looking modeling studies, the review established that ecological niche models across all Shared Socioeconomic Pathways—ranging from sustainability-oriented SSP1-2.6 to fossil-fueled SSP5-8.5 scenarios—predict substantial spatial expansions of chikungunya risk by 2040, 2060, 2080, and 2100. These predictive projections consistently signal a transboundary expansion toward higher latitudes and higher altitudes, exposing immunologically naive populations in temperate zones. Predictive models indicate novel transmission risks emerging in Germany and Italy as warmer temperatures lengthen vector activity windows, while modeling for Australia indicates escalating epidemic potential by 2029 along eastern and northern coastal belts. Projections for North America indicate that climatic suitability for local transmission will extend into Canada by 2040 and 2070 under both Representative Concentration Pathway 4.5 and 8.5 scenarios. To guide policy responses, the authors formulated an integrated three-tier adaptation framework synthesizing 65 studies that addressed intervention strategies. The bottom tier focuses on foundational prevention and structural resilience, accounting for 22 percent of the adaptation literature; it encompasses urban water infrastructure improvements, habitat elimination through spatial planning, community engagement, and targeted vaccine development. The mid-tier represents predictive surveillance and early warning systems, which dominate 60 percent of documented approaches through climate-based forecasting and integrated entomological-clinical tracking. The top tier encompasses reactive emergency management, comprising 18 percent of studies, which addresses acute outbreak suppression, clinical workforce preparedness, and chemical vector control scheduled around climatic activity peaks to prevent insecticide resistance evolution. Crucially, the review identified severe geographical and economic disparities that impede equitable global health defense. Empirical studies have clustered disproportionately in Europe and South America following recent high-profile outbreaks, whereas the historical epicenter of the virus in Africa and vulnerable low-income territories remain profoundly underrepresented. When classified by World Bank income brackets, the overwhelming majority of adaptation literature originates from high-income and upper-middle-income nations focusing on sophisticated mid-tier warning systems. This leaves resource-constrained, lower-income populations without validated evidence for foundational infrastructural adaptation, underscoring an urgent imperative to direct international funding toward decentralized environmental management, empirical field trials, and cross-border One Health collaborations. supplementary_news.title: 基孔肯雅热的11个关键问题,一次说清
supplementary_news.excerpt: 基孔肯雅热是由基孔肯雅病毒引起,主要经伊蚊叮咬传播的病毒性传染病,临床表现主要为发热、皮疹、关节和肌肉疼痛,多数患者1周内会好转,但30%—40%患者关节疼痛可能会持续数月甚至数年,对生活质量造成显著长期影响。-1-基孔肯雅病毒如何传播基孔肯雅病毒主要通过携带病毒的伊蚊叮咬传播,最常见的是埃及伊蚊和白纹伊蚊。
